newsitem.title: GERMANY: German budget problems cloud recovery hopes.
newsitem.headline: German budget problems cloud recovery hopes.

text.p: Germany's budgetary problems are clouding hopes for a solid economic recovery this year, casting the hard-line Bundesbank into the unfamiliar role of a saviour who could stop growth from faltering.
Economists say fiscal measures in 1997, aimed at reducing debt in order to qualify for European economic and monetary union, could lead to slower consumption and public sector outlays.
"It is a fiscal drag and it is substantial," said Adolf Rosenstock, economist at the Industrial Bank of Japan in Frankfurt, on Thursday. "There is going to be a fiscal crunch."

The budget difficulties have wide-ranging implications for Europe's ability to adopt a single currency on schedule in 1999 and strike at the heart of what economists believe is the best "policy mix" to promote growth.
Germany faces an uphill battle to reduce its deficit to qualify for monetary union and is laying on fresh taxes at the same time that it is cutting government spending.

Economists believe that all told, Germany will slash its budget deficit by anywhere from one-half to a full percentage point of gross domestic product, draining money from the economy that would otherwise have gone towards encouraging growth.
Under the terms of the European Union's Maastricht Treaty, countries seeking to join monetary union must not have budget deficits greater than three percent of GDP.
But according to a Federal Statistics Office report last week, Germany's deficit ratio was 3.9 percent.
Economists figure that the budget cutbacks will trim about three-quarters of a percentage point off GDP this year but that figure could climb if Bonn is forced to take even harsher measures.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel hinted at such steps on Wednesday, saying that a higher-than-expected budget deficit in 1996 would lead to further belt-tightening.
"It will be necessary to continue our savings course with greater determination," Waigel said.
The Bild newspaper reported on Thursday that Waigel would slap a freeze on government spending this month.
Economists said that such a freeze would disable what they call "automatic stabilisers" in government spending, which normally lead to higher spending when the economy is weak.
"There is a risk that budget difficulties could delay the expected rebound and force a downward revision of economic forecasts," Rosenstock said. "The risk scenario is growing."

He and others said Germany's difficult fiscal situation was moving the economic spotlight down the Rhine from Bonn to Frankfurt, where the Bundesbank is facing pressure to ensure that growth remains on track.
"My bias is that monetary easing could dominate fiscal contraction," said Joachim Fels, economist at J.P. Morgan in London. "It has been able to overcome tight fiscal environments in the past."
Yet the central bank has steadily slashed interest rates over the last year to historic lows, so far with little impact. Economists urge patience.

They say cuts in interest rates normally do not reveal themselves in faster growth for three to five quarters and that the low point of this interest rate cycle was only reached in the middle of last year.

And Germany may cut its key money market rate, the repo, even further. Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp, worried about high unemployment, on Thursday said: "Even monetary policy cannot be indifferent to this situation."
Economists said the impact of lower rates was already feeding through in the form of a weaker mark which helps German exporters and also by lowering borrowing costs.
"We are starting to see a pick up in investment," said Holger Schmieding, economist at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt. "The mark shows that exports should continue to climb."
